paras: The killing of Bluford Workman was the fatal shooting of a Black deaf mute man near Newberry, South Carolina, on the night of July 29, 1880. A coroner's jury found that C. D. Burton had killed him in self-defense, although the local paper had first called the killing "a horrible outrage, without the slightest provocation." Burton was later charged with the killing and released on $700 bond to await trial.

Workman was twenty-three years old and deaf and mute, and the Newberry Herald noted that he "formerly belonged" to Madison Workman. At his death he worked for Charley Floyd, and the paper described him as "a peaceable and harmless negro."

On a Friday morning Workman was found dead in a cotton patch beside the road opposite Barnett Floyd's place, having been killed the night before. He had been shot with a pistol of about .40 calibre; the ball entered below his right shoulder, passed through his heart and lodged under the skin of his left breast, where Dr. Thompson removed it. The coverage gives no account of how the encounter began.

Coroner Longshore opened an inquest on Friday but, with witnesses absent, adjourned it to Saturday and again to Monday. On Monday afternoon the jury returned a verdict that Workman had been killed by C. D. Burton in self-defense.

Despite that verdict, Burton was afterward "charged with killing" Workman. On a Thursday in mid-August he was taken before Trial Justices Bartlett S. Golding and Joel B. Heller on a writ of habeas corpus and gave bond of $700 for his appearance at trial. No report of a trial or its outcome was found.

The Newberry Herald, the only paper with its own reporting, headed its first item "Deaf and Dumb Negro Killed" and judged from what it had learned that the killing was an unprovoked outrage. It declined to repeat "the rumors that are floating around" before the verdict and called for a strict, impartial investigation and for the guilty party to be brought to justice. When the self-defense verdict came in, the Herald added it in a single line without comment.

Two weeks later the Winnsboro News and Herald and the Anderson Intelligencer reprinted a condensed version under the heading "Shot Through the Heart," placing the self-defense verdict alongside the Herald's "horrible outrage" remark. No coverage of the killing appears in the Black press.

Accounts differ on whether Workman gave provocation: the Herald first saw none, while the coroner's jury found that Burton acted in self-defense, though the evidence behind the verdict is not reported. The bail notice dates the killing to July 30, the day the first report says the body was found.

reader.title: Killing of Bluford Workman
bases: A single named man, C. D. Burton, was found by a coroner's jury to have shot Workman, and later charged and bonded for trial; no mob, band, posse or officers took part (A1, A3).
All coverage derives from the Newberry Herald (A1, A3); the Winnsboro and Anderson items are credited reprints of it (A2, A4).

accounts.label: Newberry Herald (before the verdict)
accounts.gist: From what it had learned, the killing seemed 'a horrible outrage, without the slightest provocation' of a peaceable man; it declined to print the rumors and demanded the guilty party be brought to justice.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Workman was killed by C. D. Burton in self-defense.

accounts.label: Later legal proceedings
accounts.gist: Burton was nonetheless 'charged with killing' Workman and bonded for trial at $700.

framing.detail: The local Herald headed it 'Deaf and Dumb Negro Killed' and called the killing seemingly 'a horrible outrage' without provocation, before reporting the self-defense verdict without comment.
The Winnsboro and Anderson reprints, headed 'Shot Through the Heart', put the self-defense verdict and the 'horrible outrage' line side by side.

conflicts.note: The first report places the killing on the night before the body was found on Friday; the bail item uses the date the body was found or a loose date. The first report is more detailed.
The Herald's pre-verdict judgment rests on what it had 'learned'; the jury's verdict is sworn but its evidence is not reported, and Burton was later charged anyway (A3).
